title: An Odisha Worker Went to Moscow for a Better Life. A Ukrainian Drone Killed Him in His First Month.
excerpt: A. Rameya's death at an oil refinery exposes the invisible Indian workforce trapped in Russia's conflict zones — and raises urgent questions for every family sending a son abroad.
body:
A. Rameya left his village of Madhabandha in Odisha's Ganjam district roughly a month ago. He was young, hopeful, and headed to Russia — one of the thousands of Indian workers who have quietly filled blue-collar roles in Russian industry as Western sanctions and conscription thinned the domestic labour force. On May 17, a Ukrainian drone struck the oil refinery where he worked in the Moscow region. Rameya did not survive.

Three other Indian workers were injured in the same attack. The Indian Embassy in Moscow confirmed the incident within hours, posting on X that diplomatic officials had visited the strike site and met the injured at a local hospital. Back in Ganjam, district collector Keerthi Vasan V confirmed the death and said efforts were underway to repatriate Rameya's remains.

## A War That Was Never Supposed to Touch Them

The strike was part of a massive aerial assault by Ukrainian forces on Russian energy infrastructure. The Security Service of Ukraine confirmed it had targeted an oil refinery and two pumping stations in the Moscow region, calling the operations proof that "even the heavily protected Moscow region is not beyond reach." President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the strikes as "fully justified" in response to Russia's continued bombardment of Ukrainian cities. Russian authorities reported intercepting over 120 drones within 24 hours, with flights at Moscow airports temporarily disrupted.

For Rameya and his co-workers, the geopolitics were beside the point. They were there to earn money — drawn by wages that, even at Russian blue-collar rates, dwarf what is available in rural Odisha. The pipeline of Indian workers into Russia has grown steadily since 2022, when Western companies pulled out and Russian firms began aggressively recruiting from South Asia. Exact numbers are difficult to pin down — India's Ministry of External Affairs does not publish granular migration data for Russia — but community networks and recruitment agencies in states like Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Punjab report a sharp uptick in departures.

## The Diaspora Safety Question

Rameya's death is not the first time Indian workers have been caught in the crossfire. In 2024, at least two Indians died fighting for the Russian military after being recruited under allegedly deceptive contracts, prompting a diplomatic intervention and the eventual return of several Indians. The pattern is familiar: young men from economically distressed regions accept contracts that place them in environments far more dangerous than advertised.

For the estimated 18,000-plus Indians living in Russia, the calculus has shifted. What was once considered a relatively safe destination for migrant labour now carries the risk of drone strikes on industrial sites, particularly energy infrastructure that Ukraine has made a priority target. The Moscow region, long considered insulated from frontline violence, has become a regular target for long-range Ukrainian drones.

India's diplomatic position — maintaining ties with both Moscow and Kyiv — complicates the response. The Ministry of External Affairs has consistently urged Indian nationals in conflict zones to exercise caution, but has stopped short of issuing evacuation advisories for Russia. The embassy's rapid response to the May 17 strike suggests an institutional awareness that incidents involving Indian casualties in Russia are likely to increase.

## What Families Back Home Are Asking

In Madhabandha, the questions are more immediate. How long will it take to bring Rameya home? Who pays for the repatriation? What compensation, if any, will his family receive from the Russian employer or the Indian government?

These are questions that tens of thousands of NRI families — particularly those with relatives working in Gulf states, Southeast Asia, and now Russia — know intimately. India's emigration policy framework, designed primarily for Gulf migration, has not kept pace with the diversification of Indian labour destinations. Russia, in particular, sits in a regulatory grey zone: workers often travel on tourist or business visas, without the protections that formal emigration channels provide.

## What's Next

The Indian Embassy in Moscow has said it is coordinating with Russian authorities to assist the injured and facilitate the repatriation of Rameya's remains. The Ganjam district administration is in contact with the family. Whether the incident prompts a broader policy review — on travel advisories, recruitment regulation, or diplomatic intervention — remains to be seen. For now, a village in Odisha mourns a son who went looking for opportunity and found a war instead.
